title: Elon Musk's SpaceX Just Announced Good (and Bad) News to Apple Shareholders
detail:
Elon Musk's SpaceX Just Announced Good (and Bad) News to Apple Shareholders
Adam Spatacco, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 12:20 PM CDT 5 min read
SPCX
AAPL
NVDA
VZ
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Elon Musk has spent his career challenging established industries, from payments to automobiles to space exploration. His latest ambitions could create unexpected tailwinds and headwinds for one of the world's most valuable companies: Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL).

Last week, Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), better known as SpaceX, announced plans to acquire nationwide wireless spectrum, bringing its Starlink satellite business closer to competing with Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

At first glance, that sounds like bad news for telecommunications companies, not for Apple. However, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan identified three ways Starlink could threaten the iPhone maker's business. While I see Mohan's points, there's a way Starlink may benefit Apple in the near term.

Image source: Getty Images.
SpaceX wants to disrupt the wireless industry

Most Americans buy cellular service through Verizon, AT&T, or T-Mobile. These companies operate networks that connect smartphones through ground-based cell towers. SpaceX wants to challenge that business model.

The company's Starlink Mobile initiative aims to combine satellite connectivity with traditional wireless infrastructure, allowing consumers to receive cellular service across a larger geographic area. To support this vision, SpaceX plans to acquire approximately $8 billion worth of low-frequency wireless spectrum.

Wireless companies need access to frequencies to transmit calls, messages, and internet data. The frequencies SpaceX is acquiring are attractive because they cover long distances and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. When combined with Starlink's satellite network, they could help SpaceX develop an alternative to incumbent wireless carriers.

This is a big deal because SpaceX won't necessarily need to replicate every aspect of traditional cellular infrastructure. But building a reliable nationwide network requires substantial capital expenditures, regulatory approvals, technical execution, and customer adoption.

How does Starlink threaten Apple?

To understand the risk to Apple, investors need to consider how Americans buy smartphones. Rather than charging the full price for a new phone upfront, a wireless carrier usually offers a promotional credit if you trade in your existing device and agree to remain on its network. Essentially, you pay the difference for the new phone, and the promotional credit is typically distributed across your monthly bills. Interestingly, Apple still receives the phone's true selling price. Wireless providers absorb the promotional subsidy because retaining a paying subscriber can be financially worthwhile in the long run.

A suit for two 2024 AT&T data breaches has been court-approved for a $177 million settlement, and if you claimed, you could be getting a check soon.

The settlement is related to two separate data incidents that occurred in March and July of 2024, where parties agreed to settle together.

Is it too late to get an AT&T settlement payment?

The claim period for this settlement has already closed, and the settlement has been approved in court.

If you failed to file a claim or had your claim denied, you won't get a payment.

When will AT&T settlement payments be sent out?

According to the settlement agreement, payment should be distributed within 60 days of the effective date of the agreement.

The court approved the settlement on Oct. 2, but there may be appeals to resolve before checks are sent.

How will I get my AT&T settlement payment?

Payments will be sent via paper check or electronically.

How much is my settlement check?

Per settlement documents, the estimated tiered payment amounts are as follows:

AT&T 1 - Tier 1 = $39 - $40AT&T 2 - Tier 2 = $7.50 - $8.10AT&T 2 - Tier 3 = $6.50 - $7.10

The market expects AT&T (T) to deliver a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. This widely-known consensus outlook is important in assessing the company's earnings picture, but a powerful factor that might influence its near-term stock price is how the actual results compare to these estimates.

The earnings report, which is expected to be released on October 21, might help the stock move higher if these key numbers are better than expectations. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.

While management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call will mostly determine the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations, it's worth having a handicapping insight into the odds of a positive EPS surprise.

Zacks Consensus Estimate

This telecommunications company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $0.61 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +13%.

Revenues are expected to be $31.68 billion, up 3.2% from the year-ago quarter.

Estimate Revisions Trend

The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 4.4% lower over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.

Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for T
Earnings Whisper

Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

title: Elon Musk Says SpaceX Just Bought "the Last Critical Piece" Required to Take on the Wireless Giants. Here's Why It Will Need to Spend Billions More to Compete.
detail:
Elon Musk Says SpaceX Just Bought "the Last Critical Piece" Required to Take on the Wireless Giants. Here's Why It Will Need to Spend Billions More to Compete.
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 6 min read
SPCX
NVDA
T
VZ
TMUS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) is threatening to upend yet another industry. This time, the company has the wireless communication sector in its sights, as it has now acquired what Elon Musk described as "the last critical piece" of the puzzle required to offer complete wireless coverage in America. Shares of the big three wireless carriers -- AT&T (NYSE: T), T-Mobile (NASDAQ: TMUS), and Verizon (NYSE: VZ) -- fell sharply on the news that SpaceX intends to compete in their arena.

However, SpaceX's latest big purchase could also be sending it down a path that will require it to spend billions of dollars more. While it's not a meaningful competitive threat to the wireless carriers yet, it could still have a significant effect on their finances as soon as next year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What did SpaceX just buy?

SpaceX has agreed to acquire 14 megahertz (MHz) of paired spectrum licenses in the 800 MHz band from Grain Management for a reported $8 billion. These are spectrum licenses T-Mobile had to give up as part of its merger with Sprint. The spectrum is particularly good for transmissions covering long (unobstructed) distances and penetrating buildings. That's what makes it so valuable to SpaceX, which has so far been limited to connecting to devices outdoors with its Starlink satellite constellation.

The new spectrum licenses will join SpaceX's existing licenses in the 2-gigahertz (GHz) spectrum band, which its new V2 Starlink satellites will use. However, if SpaceX truly wants to compete with the established wireless carriers, it will need a lot more spectrum.

It shouldn't be ignored that T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T aren't standing still. Earlier this year, the three formed a joint venture to expand their satellite direct-to-device wireless coverage. AT&T and Verizon have partnered with AST SpaceMobile, which is building a constellation of satellites to cover mobile dead zones. T-Mobile currently partners with SpaceX. The new joint venture aims to expand the number of satellite service providers the carriers work with.

In other words, the carriers are looking to offer the same type of unified service that SpaceX plans to, but to get there first. They already have access to the scarcest resource necessary to fulfill that goal: wireless spectrum. As mentioned, the low-band spectrum in the 800 MHz band that SpaceX is buying is good for covering long distances and penetrating buildings. However, it can't handle much traffic. That makes it good for providing coverage in rural areas, but not as good for more urban areas. Having a full breadth of spectrum, and a lot of it, is necessary for any wireless network that intends to compete nationwide.

AT&T Exits Mexico for $2 Billion: Why Taking Less Still Makes Sense ©teekid from Getty Images Signature and Miguel Á. Padriñán from Pexels via Canva

AT&T (T:NYSE) agreed on Tuesday, October 13, to sell AT&T Mexico to a 50/50 consortium of Grupo Televisa (TV) and Fintech Holdings for $2 billion in cash, plus contractual and contingent benefits. The deal should close in the first quarter of 2027, pending regulatory approvals in Mexico.

The $2 billion cash consideration is less than half the combined headline values of AT&T's entry deals: $2.5 billion for Iusacell and $1.875 billion for Nextel Mexico. Both acquisitions closed in 2015, with payments reduced by net debt and other adjustments.

Why AT&T Will Take Less for Mexico

The unit grew sales but never earned much. Revenue rose 59% from $2.75 billion in 2021 to $4.38 billion in 2025. Operating income only turned positive in 2024, and last year's $145 million was a 3.3% margin.

T Latin America Operating Income and Operating Revenue (TIKR)

Across those five years, the business ran a cumulative operating loss of about $790 million. The $2 billion cash consideration is roughly 14 times last year's operating profit, and AT&T says the sale will sharpen its capital-allocation focus on U.S. fiber and 5G.

That's the same goal behind the fiber joint venture AT&T signed with GIP and CPP Investments a week earlier.

The Street Won't Rewrite Its AT&T Math Over This
T Stock Street Targets (TIKR)

Analysts were already cooling on AT&T before the sale. The mean target was $28.76 on October 13, about 26% above that day's $22.85 close but down from $30.66 at the end of September 2025. Ratings now show 11 buys, 3 outperforms, 10 holds and 1 sell. A year earlier, there were 7 outperforms and only 6 holds.

Selling a business with $145 million in annual operating income makes AT&T simpler and concentrates its investment case further on U.S. connectivity. Holds have risen from 6 to 10, showing a more cautious ratings mix, though the ratings alone don't establish why analysts became less bullish.

title: How Much Could You Lose In T-Mobile Stock?
detail:
How Much Could You Lose In T-Mobile Stock?
Trefis Team
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 6:56 PM CDT 4 min read
TMUS
^GSPC
T
SPCX
VZ

Image from Pixabay

T-Mobile US (TMUS) stock fell 16.7% over the past month, diverging from a 2.0% gain for the S&P 500. News reports tied a sharp drop on October 9 to a SpaceX spectrum deal, and AT&T, Verizon and Comcast each lost more than 12% over the same month. You may still think of a wireless carrier as a stock that holds up in a selloff. So how far has T-Mobile stock fallen in past market selloffs?

T-Mobile Stock's 54% Drop In 2011, Much Of It In One Day

T-Mobile stock recorded its steepest fall in a market shock since 2007 during the US debt ceiling crisis. From July to October 2011, the shares fell 54%, compared with an 18% decline for the S&P 500 over the same months. Market pressure alone does not fully explain the drop. The shares fell from $20.38 to $12.92 on August 2, 2011, a 37% drop in one day.

The 2008-2009 financial crisis marked the next steepest drop. T-Mobile stock fell 47% during that time, a milder decline than the 53% loss for the S&P 500. Over a longer stretch, from a peak in 2007 to a low in 2010, the stock fell 86%.

Historically, T-Mobile stock has traded through 15 market shocks since 2007. A typical event has been much milder. The stock fell 18.0% on average across these shocks, compared with 15.8% for the index. On average, the shares have dropped slightly more than the broader market.

How Long Did T-Mobile Stock Take To Recover?

The median recovery time from a low was 3.7 months, though four rebounds took more than a year. T-Mobile ultimately returned to its pre-shock high after 13 of the 14 shocks in which it fell. The stock needed 20.6 months to recover from the 2011 decline, a window that includes the one-day break in price. Following the credit crunch of summer 2007, a full recovery required 111.2 months.

Only one recovery remains unfinished. T-Mobile stock is still 43% below the high it reached before the 2025 tariff shock.

Which Of T-Mobile's Numbers Are Getting Worse?

Several underlying metrics are weakening. T-Mobile reported a slipping profit margin, slower sales growth in the latest quarter, and elevated debt compared with the broader market. The company retained 20% of its sales as operating profit over the past twelve months, down from 23% a year earlier. Sales grew 7.9% in the latest quarter from a year before, a deceleration from the 10.6% growth in the prior quarter. T-Mobile currently carries debt equal to 72.6% of its market value, against 21% for the S&P 500.

Looking toward the third quarter, whose results are still pending, management forecast fewer net new accounts and slower profit growth. During the July 23, 2026 call, the company projected about 250,000 net new postpaid accounts, down from a net 277,000 in the second quarter. Management also forecast an 8% year-over-year increase in core adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure the company guides to. This marks a step down from the 12% growth reported during that call. Management said the slowdown reflects the timing of last year's acquisitions.
